creator: Sabine Hossenfelder
title: AI Is Taking Over Physics and Nobody Talks About It
full_text:
Artificial intelligence has eaten maths
and now it's coming for physics and the
interesting bit is no one's talking
about it. So, let's talk about it. In
maths things have been happening so
fast. I've given up trying to keep you
updated. Since we last talked about it,
Claude Fable 5 helped find a counter
example to the Jacobian conjecture which
I never heard of but can now tell you
that it had been open since 1939.
Then OpenAI announced 10 results from
its still unreleased Astra model, each
of which either solved or advanced
long-standing open problem. At least
that's what they say. Another group used
chat GPT to disprove a 30-year-old
conjecture that no one had heard of
previously either and earlier this month
Anthropic announced that Claude had made
a major advance on the Riemann zeta
function, so working towards the Riemann
hypothesis. Finally, a topic that even I
have heard of. I think at this point
most math mathematicians have accepted
that large language models are now
capable of serious math. It seems likely
to me that mathematics will be entirely
automated in the near future and
especially young people just entering
the field are caught between depression
and anger. Graduate student Tasman Chu
thinks that mathematics is in an
existential crisis and calls for a
moratorium on using LLMs to prove novel
mathematical theorems. Assistant
Professor Maximilian Reich has written a
preprint in which he makes the case for
total opposition to the use of
artificial intelligence in mathematics.
Postdoc Alexis Machete argues that LLMs
are evil because they contribute to the
climate crisis and PhD student Kerwin
Hampshire thinks he's going insane and
is suffering a profound spiritual crisis
due to these developments.
Mathematicians have independently
derived the same existential crisis by
four different methods. Assistant
Professor Daniel Litt, meanwhile, has
given a more or less serious talk about
the end of mathematics, in which he
belabors that AI will lead to the
production of mathematically correct
results that no one will read, no one
will care about, and no one will benefit
from academic business as usual. But,
what about physics? If AI is now good
enough to lead math proofs, then it
should also be good enough to do physics
calculations. In fact, it is. I know
this because I've tried. I also know
that a lot of theoretical physicists are
now doing the same thing, taking
research ideas that they haven't had
time to follow through and put them into
AI to see what comes out. And sometimes
the result is verifiably good enough for
publication. Peter Woit has looked at
the number of submissions to the archive
preprint server in the category hep-th,
that's high energy physics theory, and
finds that it's up about 30%
in May and June compared to previous
years. One of the recent examples comes
from quantum physics. Physicists in this
area have long wondered if there's an
easier way to create some complicated
entangled states. Gerardo Adesso at the
University of Nottingham has now proved
that the answer is no, and he did so
with the help of ChatGPT 5.6, about
which he says the AI made a central
contribution to developing the proof
strategy. He then checked every step of
the final proof himself. Another recent
example goes all the way back to James
Clerk Maxwell. Imagine a collection of
electric charges in random places.
There'll be some places where their
electric forces exactly cancel, kind of
like Lagrange points in gravity. Maxwell
proposed a rule for how many such places
you could get from a given number of
charges. Three researchers have now
shown that Maxwell's rule is wrong. And
their paper says the idea behind this
construction was suggested again by chat
GPT 5.6. Those two examples are still
very mathematical. So, here is one
involving an experiment. These two
researchers were studying how tiny
silicon membranes behave if you shine on
them with a laser. For they stated
measurements and developed a model about
which they write that it was derived
with the help of Claude Fable 5. The
model has excellent agreement with the
observations. I could go on like this
for a while. There's a paper in high
energy physics that used several large
language models to carry out the
symbolic and high precision numerical
computations. Another paper in quantum
physics used Claude for numerical
calculations. Another team had Claude
write software for moving ions around
inside a quantum computer. And in fusion
research, a chat GPT agent was put in
charge of deciding which stellarator
designs to try next. Physicists have
clearly picked up on the LLM maths
revolution, but it's happening in a
completely different way. They just
organically integrate the models as
tools and move on.
I also haven't yet seen the same
desperation as I have seen among young
mathematicians. Mathematicians see
artificial intelligence and ask whether
mathematics will survive.
Physicists ask whether they can finish
the calculation by Friday. A few years
ago, I received some ugly letters from a
debt collection company. They threatened
to sue me for ordering something online
and then not paying it. Turned out that
someone had stolen my private data. I
managed to get out of this, but since
then I've become very protective of my
personal information, which is why I've
signed up to Incogni, who've been
sponsoring this video. Each time you
open a website, it'll try to collect
data about who you are and where you are
and what other websites you've visited.
Many firms then make money by selling
your private information to data
brokers. Most countries have laws
against that and you can ask for your
data to be removed, but doing this takes
up a lot of time. Incogni auto mates the
process of getting you out of those
databases. You sign up and they'll
contact the big sinners request that
your personal details be removed.
They'll keep on doing that and if you
want, send you updates about the
progress they're making. They now also
have a custom removal feature where you
can submit specific websites. I'll be
using this a lot. Incogni has really
made my life better. If that sounds like
something you could need to, use my link
Sabina or the custom link in the info
because the first 100 people to use it
will get 60% off. Stay safe. Thanks for
watching. See you tomorrow.

notes.note: The real essay behind this is Kirwin Hampshire's "Dark Night of Mathematics." His spiritual crisis stemmed from LLMs solving major math conjectures, not climate change. No evidence exists of a postdoc named Alexis Machete making a climate-based "LLMs are evil" argument.
notes.claim: Postdoc Alexis Machete argued that LLMs are evil because they contribute to the climate crisis.
notes.context_quote: Postdoc Alexis Machete argues that LLMs are evil because they contribute to the climate crisis
notes.context_paragraph: Postdoc Alexis Machete argues that LLMs are evil because they contribute to the climate crisis and PhD student Kerwin Hampshire thinks he's going insane and is suffering a profound spiritual crisis due to these developments.

sources.quote: I am suffering a profound spiritual crisis due to these developments. I have been screaming internally for days. It feels as though I am living inside of a nightmare.
sources.explanation: Kirwin Hampshire confirms he is the author suffering a spiritual crisis.

sources.quote: During the last week or so LLMs have produced a number of counterexamples to significant long-standing conjectures.
sources.explanation: The source identifies the cause of the crisis as LLMs solving mathematical conjectures, not climate change.

sources.quote: a PhD student in pure mathematics named Kirwin Hampshire, confessed to having a ‘spiritual crisis’ over the threat of AI taking away the most meaningful part of his work.
sources.explanation: The source corroborates that the crisis is about the nature of mathematical work and discovery, not environmental concerns.

notes.note: Kirwin Hampshire's essay "The Dark Night of Mathematics" attributes his crisis to LLMs producing counterexamples to long-standing math conjectures, not a climate debate. No postdoc named "Alexis Machete" appears in his essay; his name is spelled "Kirwin," not "Kerwin."
notes.claim: PhD student Kerwin Hampshire stated he is suffering a profound spiritual crisis due to AI developments in mathematics.
notes.context_quote: PhD student Kerwin Hampshire thinks he's going insane and is suffering a profound spiritual crisis due to these developments.
notes.context_paragraph: Postdoc Alexis Machete argues that LLMs are evil because they contribute to the climate crisis and PhD student Kerwin Hampshire thinks he's going insane and is suffering a profound spiritual crisis due to these developments.

sources.explanation: The title confirms the author's name is spelled "Kirwin," not "Kerwin."

sources.quote: I am suffering a profound spiritual crisis due to these developments.
sources.explanation: Hampshire attributes his crisis to LLMs producing counterexamples to math conjectures, as mentioned in his opening paragraph.

sources.quote: I am going insane. During the last week or so LLMs have produced a number of counterexamples to significant long-standing conjectures.
sources.explanation: This establishes the actual cause of his distress, which is mathematical progress by AI, not a climate debate.

sources.quote: Mathematician Kirwin Hampshire published an impassioned essay last week, The Dark Night of Mathematics, describing "a profound spiritual crisis" brought on by previous (and less significant) results.
sources.explanation: Confirms the spelling of the name and the topic of the essay (math results vs spiritual crisis).

notes.note: The preprint's actual author is Max Weinreich, not "Maximilian Reich." His paper "The crisis of AI-generated mathematics" argues for total opposition to AI in mathematics, matching the described thesis, but the name in this clip is incorrect.
notes.claim: Assistant Professor Maximilian Reich wrote a preprint arguing for total opposition to the use of artificial intelligence in mathematics.

Confirms the author's name is Max Weinreich, not Maximilian Reich.
